name: Medical tourism (Turkey/Istanbul/Korea)

card.summary: Travelling abroad, often to Turkey or South Korea, for cosmetic surgery, hair transplants or dental work at lower prices; reviews flag infection and follow-up-care risks.
card.aka: Turkey trip, cosmetic tourism, health tourism
card.note: Published literature on medical tourism documents infectious complications, limited aftercare and insurance gaps; outcomes vary widely by clinic.

quick.overview:
Medical tourism means travelling to another country to obtain non-emergency medical care. In appearance culture the term usually refers to surgery, hair transplants and dental work in places such as Istanbul, Antalya or South Korea, where prices can be lower than in the patient's home country.

There are no controlled trials of 'looksmaxxing trips' as such. Public-health reviews of medical tourism in general describe benefits such as access and cost, alongside complications and continuity-of-care problems.
quick.mechanism: Patients usually book through clinics or agents, travel for a package that can include surgery, accommodation and transfers, and return home within days to weeks. Follow-up care after return is arranged with local clinicians, if at all.
quick.risks: Reviews report infections (including outbreaks of fungal meningitis linked to cosmetic surgery in Mexico), difficulty arranging follow-up, and possible clotting risks with long flights after surgery. Legal recourse and insurance coverage for complications can be limited. Regulation differs by country; Turkey introduced a regulation on international health tourism in 2017.

lead: Medical tourism is travel abroad to obtain medical treatment. Historically it meant patients from poorer countries seeking care in wealthy ones; more recently it often means patients from high-income countries travelling to lower-cost destinations, usually for surgery, dental work or fertility treatment, with cosmetic surgery a large category. [1][2]

In appearance-focused communities, Turkey (especially Istanbul and Antalya) is known for hair transplants and dental veneers and crowns, and South Korea for facial cosmetic surgery. [1] A 2024 ISAPS analysis of global aesthetic statistics reported 34.9 million surgical and nonsurgical aesthetic procedures by plastic surgeons in 2023 and included questions on the prevalence of medical tourism. [3]

Academic reviews note that medical tourism is growing and that infectious complications and continuity of care are recurring concerns. [4][5] The evidence base consists mainly of reviews, case series and scoping studies rather than trials.

paras: Scholars distinguish several forms of cross-border patient mobility, and a typology paper sets out the categories, while some authors prefer the broader phrase 'movement for healthcare'. [6][7] A scoping review of patient experience found that little was known about its scope, and a separate scoping review examined its effects on destination and departure countries. [8][9]

Turkey is described as an affordable hub for hair transplants, and dental treatments such as veneers, crowns and implants are offered in Istanbul, Ankara and Antalya. [1] Roughly 178,000 health tourists visited in the first half of 2018, according to figures summarized by Wikipedia, with about two-thirds treated in private hospitals. [1] Turkey's Regulation on International Health Tourism took effect on 13 July 2017, and the Ministry of Health established USHAS in 2019 to promote and regulate the sector. [1]
South Korea appears in general lists of popular cosmetic-surgery destinations. [1] The sources reviewed give no detailed data specific to its cosmetic sector.

No studies found of travel for appearance procedures to Turkey or South Korea as a defined intervention. Related research covers medical tourism generally: reviews of infectious complications, scoping reviews of patient experience, and registered trials that look at venous changes during long-haul flights after aesthetic surgery. [4][8][10][11]

A 2024 review of the previous 18 months found an increase in reported infectious complications in patients who had received care abroad, often with prolonged morbidity, repeat treatment and hospital stays, and occasionally deaths. It described an outbreak of fungal meningitis in US residents who had epidural anesthesia for cosmetic surgery in two Mexican clinics: 31 cases with severe cerebrovascular complications and eight deaths as of July 2023. [4]

A 2019 JAMA article reviewed infections linked to medical tourism, and other papers discuss the risk of carrying multi-resistant bacteria between healthcare systems and the spread of resistant organisms in destinations that are major medical-tourism hubs. [12][13][14]

General travel and medical-tourism sources also list unfamiliar local infections, variable post-operative care, limited follow-up after return, flights shortly after surgery raising clot risks, and difficulty obtaining insurance cover or legal remedies. [1][5]

Registered studies include observational and randomized work on popliteal vein diameter during long-haul flights after aesthetic surgery and a study of anxiety in bariatric health tourism. [10][11][15]
